title: The Three Stages of Emigration Grief: An Academic's Guide to Learning the Australian Education System
author: Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes maps her own experience emigrating from England to Australia as an education academic onto three stages of professional grief: honeymoon, devastation and confusion, and finally pragmatism and hope. In the honeymoon stage, unfamiliar acronyms (AITSL, NESA, VIT, QCT, APST, LANTITE) feel charming rather than burdensome, and cross-system comparisons feel like intellectual sport. In the devastation stage, she confronts a specific and disorienting form of professional loss: she doesn't just lack knowledge, she has the wrong kind of knowledge, and constantly translating Australian systems into English equivalents ('is this basically Ofsted?') becomes a trap that prevents her from understanding the new system on its own terms. The grief here is subtle but real — losing the 'folklore,' the twenty years of invisible policy history that lets insiders hear subtext where newcomers only hear the sentence — which is destabilizing precisely because being knowledgeable was central to her professional identity. The essay resolves in a hard-won pragmatism: once she stops asking 'what's the English equivalent' and starts asking 'how does this actually work here,' she regains both competence and the capacity to contribute rather than just cope, closing with the image of paying the lesson forward to a newly arrived colleague experiencing Stage Two in real time.
points: Hughes's sharpest diagnostic insight is that the disorientation of professional emigration isn't a lack of knowledge but a mismatch of knowledge — 'the first shock is not that you know nothing, it is that you know quite a lot, but not necessarily the right things.'

She identifies cross-system comparison as simultaneously the natural coping mechanism and the trap: 'the temptation to compare is enormous... you spend so much time trying to work out what something is the Australian equivalent of that you fail to understand what it actually is.'

The specific loss she names — missing the 'folklore,' the twenty years of policy history that lets insiders hear subtext where newcomers only hear the literal sentence — gives a precise vocabulary for a kind of professional grief rarely named directly.

The resolution turns on a single reframed question, from 'what is the English equivalent?' to 'how does this work here, and why?' — a transferable technique for any professional navigating an unfamiliar institutional system, not just international emigrants.
quotes: My experience of adjusting to Australian education and teacher education has broadly involved three stages: honeymoon, devastation and confusion, and finally, pragmatism and hope.
AITSL, NESA, VIT, QCT, APST, LANTITE — they seem less like an administrative obstacle and more like an interesting new dialect of a language you already speak.
The first shock is not that you know nothing. It is that you know quite a lot, but not necessarily the right things.
The temptation to compare is enormous because comparison is how we make the unfamiliar intelligible. Unfortunately, it can also become a trap.
In Australia, you may understand the published policy perfectly well while missing the twenty years of history sitting invisibly behind it. Everyone else hears the subtext; you hear the sentence.
You stop asking, "What is the English equivalent?" and start asking, "How does this work here, and why?" That small shift changes everything.
You stop trying to recreate the professional world you left behind and start contributing to the one you are now part of.
